thread:
Miguel (AcmeCorp): Hey team — after moving our workload to the private VPC gateway we've started seeing intermittent 429s during our nightly batch ingest. It looks bursty: jobs start fine but ~3–5 minutes in we get a flood of 429s for a subset of requests. No auth failures in our logs, tokens accepted earlier in the run. Any pointers?

Aisha (Support): Sorry you're hitting that, Miguel. Quick Qs: are you on Redwood-managed gateway or customer-managed? Did you change ingress class / egress proxy recently? Also, do the 429s include Retry-After headers?

Miguel (AcmeCorp): We're on a customer-managed gateway (k8s nginx ingress in our VPC). No recent changes except we scaled the batch job from 4->12 replicas last week. 429s do include Retry-After sometimes, sometimes not. Example response body: `{ "error": "rate_limit_exceeded", "detail": "token_bucket_full" }`.

Raj (SRE): scaling replicas is a classic burst cause — more concurrency hitting the gateway at once. Two places to check: (1) ingress NGINX / Envoy rate limit config on the gateway (2) any Redis-backed global rate limiter if you've installed one. Also check kube-proxy conntrack and node-level conn limits.

Olga (Runtime Eng): Can you share the exact ingress class and annotations on the service + the gateway config? If you're using nginx-ingress, the annotations that matter: `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps`, `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-burst`, and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections`. If those are low, bursts from scaling will overflow the token bucket quickly.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): Ingress annotations: `limit-rps: "50"`, `limit-burst: "20"`, connections not set. We're also fronted by an internal ALB in front of the ingress. I'll paste relevant YAML in a sec.

Aisha (Support): Two troubleshooting paths: repro locally with a controlled burst to observe 429 cross-sections, and gather metrics/trace-id from Redwood responses so we can correlate on our side (if the 429s include Redwood trace id). Also check whether your gateway is returning 429s or Redwood's VPC gateway. The `via` header or `x-redwood-server` in responses sometimes reveals that.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): Sample curl loop we ran: 
```bash
for i in {1..300}; do \\curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -X POST https://private-gw.acme/api/generate &
done
wait
```
We see ~60% 200s then a sudden jump to 429 for ~40s then it recovers.

Raj (SRE): That reproduces a classic token-bucket exhaustion. Quick diagnostic commands: `kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx -o wide` to confirm pod count; `kubectl logs` of the ingress controller around the time of the 429 to see `limit` lines; and `kubectl describe svc` for endpoints. Also check node-level `ulimit` and conntrack: `cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max` and `ss -s`.

Olga (Runtime Eng): On the Redwood side there are two important guardrails: per-API-key concurrency and per-IP rate caps. In Private deployments we push some of the enforcement into the customer gateway to avoid incurring extra latency. If your gateway is configured to send `x-forwarded-for` correctly, Redwood will attribute and apply per-customer quotas. If the ALB+ingress aren't preserving client IPs, you could be hitting per-node limits instead of per-caller.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): We are using proxy protocol on the ALB -> ingress. XFF seems present. What exact Redis/Envoy config would you recommend for smoothing bursts?

Olga (Runtime Eng): If you run an Envoy rate limit service (RLS) backed by Redis, use token-bucket with a high `burst` and a modest refill rate. Example Envoy filter snippet (pseudo):
```yaml
- name: envoy.filters.http.ratelimit
  config: 
    domain: redwood_private
    stage: 0
    rate_limit_service:
      grpc_service:
        envoy_grpc:
          cluster_name: rls
````
And Redis keys should use `leaky_bucket` semantics with TTLs matching your burst window.

Raj (SRE): For a quick mitigation, bump nginx `limit-burst` to something like 200–400 while you tune (if your backend can accept higher concurrency). Also add `limit-connections` so a single client can't open hundreds of keepalive sockets. Example annotations we applied for another customer: `limit-rps: "200"`, `limit-burst: "300"`, `limit-connections: "1000"` (tweak to cluster size).

Miguel (AcmeCorp): Ok will try that. One more: could this look like billing/quota exhaustion on Redwood side? We saw a sudden drop in throughput for a few minutes once.

Ken (Billing): If your plan quota is exhausted you typically get clear error JSON: `quota_exceeded` and billing events show usage spikes. 429s alone don't prove billing issue; we'll cross-check your account usage for the timestamps (if you share trace IDs we can match).

Aisha (Support): Can you grab the response headers for a 429 occurrence? We look for: `x-redwood-trace-id`, `x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining`, `Retry-After`, and `via`. That will tell us whether the rate-limiter is in Redwood or at your ingress.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): Pasted one 429 response headers: 
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 3
x-redwood-trace-id: 9f3b2c7a
x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining: 0
via: 1.1 nginx
```
Seems nginx returned it (via: 1.1 nginx) but x-redwood headers present too which is odd.

Olga (Runtime Eng): That suggests layered rate limiting: both Redwood and your gateway are emitting headers. If nginx is returning the 429 it will add `via: nginx`. Sometimes the ingress is configured to short-circuit when `x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining: 0` is present — i.e., nginx is interpreting the downstream header and returning early. Which NGINX module are you using for rate limiting? `limit_req_module`? If so, some setups inspect upstream headers to decide.

Raj (SRE): Action plan: (1) Temporarily increase `limit-burst` + `limit-rps` on ingress for the batch window; (2) enable rate-limit metrics on ingress to gather RPS/429 counters; (3) run controlled repro and capture a 429 with headers (we need `x-redwood-trace-id`); (4) Ken to check account quotas for those trace timestamps.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): Doing step 1 now — patching ingress to `limit-rps: "300"`, `limit-burst: "500"`. Patching... done. Rerunning curl script.

IncidentBot: New escalation created INC-9023 (priority P2) — linking thread 1780501234 to the incident.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): After bumping burst settings the run completed with 98% 200s, a handful of 429s scattered. Looks much better.

Olga (Runtime Eng): Great. For long-term: 1) implement smoothing via a client-side backoff + jitter (stop blasting replicas concurrently), 2) consider a shared leaky-bucket in the gateway (Redis RLS), 3) set cluster-wide HPA/Pod disruption budgets to ramp replicas gradually instead of instant scaling, and 4) expose a per-route concurrency semaphore in the gateway to limit spikes.

Ken (Billing): We checked usage — there was a burst spike but not a quota hit. We didn't see billing-blocking events.

Aisha (Support): If you want we can run a quick config review with runtime Eng (Olga) and SRE (Raj) tomorrow to look at ingress + ALB settings, warm-up policies, and a recommended nginx/Envoy config.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): Yes please — a config review would be great. Also: can Redwood provide an example Envoy RLS + Redis setup you recommend for private VPC customers?

Olga (Runtime Eng): I'll drop an example RLS guide in a follow-up thread (Redis schema, sample envoy filter, HPA tuning recommendations). For now, two snippets that help:

1) nginx ingress annotation to avoid short-circuiting on upstream headers: `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-ignore-headers: "x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining"`

2) simple leaky bucket pseudocode to implement in Redis: 
```python
# key = rate:<client_id>
now = time()
tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now - last_ts) * refill_rate)
if tokens >= 1: tokens -= 1; allow; else: deny (429)
```

I'll attach the full guide to INC-9023.

Miguel (AcmeCorp): Thanks all — warming up the cluster and will follow up after config review. :thumbsup:

Aisha (Support): Closing loop here once you confirm the scheduled review. Marking this thread for handoff to INC-9023. :white_check_mark:
